theme: Glorious things of you are spoken, O city of God
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 87. This short psalm is a song about Zion and the nations. Read it slowly. It makes a surprising claim about who belongs to God’s city.
settingTheScene: Psalm 87 is another psalm of the sons of Korah and another song of Zion. It is only seven verses, and it is one of the most unusual psalms. It names the great enemies of Israel (Rahab, Babylon, Philistia, Tyre, Cush) and declares that people from these nations will be counted as born in Zion. It looks forward to the day the nations share in the blessing of God.
observation: “On the holy mount stands the city he founded” (v. 1).
“The LORD loves the gates of Zion more than all the dwelling places of Jacob” (v. 2).
“Glorious things of you are spoken, O city of God” (v. 3).
“Among those who know me I mention Rahab and Babylon; behold, Philistia and Tyre, with Cush: This one was born there” (v. 4).
“And of Zion it shall be said, This one and that one were born in her” (v. 5).
“For the Most High himself will establish her” (v. 5).
“The LORD records as he registers the peoples, This one was born there” (v. 6).
“Singers and dancers alike say, All my springs are in you” (v. 7).
interpretation:
This psalm turns expectations upside down. Rahab is a poetic name for Egypt. Babylon, Philistia, Tyre, and Cush are the major powers around Israel, and most of them were Israel’s enemies. In the psalm, God says that he will count them among “those who know me.” People from those nations will be said to have been born in Zion.

Being “born in Zion” means being a full citizen, a native of God’s city. The psalm imagines the LORD keeping a register. As he reads the list, he says of Egyptians, Babylonians, Philistines, and Ethiopians, “This one was born there.” It is a vision of grace beyond Israel. The people who were enemies become citizens of the city of God. The wall of separation is broken.

Why is this so important? It reflects the promise to Abraham that all nations would be blessed (Genesis 12:3). It anticipates the prophets, who spoke of the nations streaming to Zion (Isaiah 2:2-3). The Davidic covenant was not simply for Israel’s benefit. God’s purpose was a family drawn from every nation.

The last verse ties it together. “All my springs are in you.” The singers and dancers find all their joy in Zion. For those who are born there, it is the source of life itself.

This psalm shows how the Old Testament prepares for the gospel. It is not a late idea that the nations are welcome. It was always God’s plan. When Peter and Paul preach to the Gentiles, they are fulfilling what psalms like this foretold.
connection: Galatians 4:26 speaks of “the Jerusalem above” as our mother. Ephesians 2:19 says, “You are no longer strangers and aliens, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God.” Jesus said, “You must be born again” (John 3:7). Philippians 3:20 says, “Our citizenship is in heaven.” Revelation 7:9 pictures a multitude from every nation standing before the throne.
application:
Thank God that you are a citizen of his city, whatever your background.

Ask whether you have drawn lines around who belongs. Is there a group you consider an outsider?

Pray for a nation that seems far from God, that people from it would be counted as born in Zion.
prayerPrompts: Thank God for counting you as born in Zion.
Ask him to make you welcoming to those who are far off.
Pray that people from every nation would belong to him.
